Rosetta Logos

The Logos Manifold: the mean space of human languages, computed from real word embeddings and a word list built by linguists. Every number here was measured.

Arms of the mean space

groups of concepts that sit together, found in full dimension from all languages. Each arm holds words that can stand in for one another in a sentence, and several are whole parts of speech: numbers, actions, pointing words, qualities. Every arm is tighter inside than outside in at least of the languages. Tick Arms above to draw them; choose one to isolate it.

Tightness is the average similarity between an arm's members (0 = unrelated, 1 = identical). The names are my labels for each group. In this flattened view arms overlap; in full dimension they are separate.

How close each language sits to the mean of the others

Each language is compared with a mean built without it, then scored against its own shuffled baseline. 0 means no better than chance, 1 means identical shape. This table uses languages on the concepts they all share.

Mostly a measure of text volume

The number of distinct words a language's training text contained explains of the differences in this ranking. Languages with little text online sit far from the mean whatever their history. Sort by Beyond text volume to see what is left.

Beyond the first 60 languages

Three tests on wider data. The first uses 49 languages from a parallel Bible corpus (the same verses in each), the second uses 147 Indo-European languages with expert cognate judgements, and the third uses word lists for about 10,000 languages. They measure different things, so they are shown separately.

1 · Meaning shape, 49 languages

Equal text for each language (320,000 words), concepts taken from the words of one anchor language and matched through the parallel verses. Does a language's nearest neighbour belong to its own family?

AnchorBlockNearest is a relativeNearer by
English48 × 5775% (chance 39%)3.9%
Hebrew46 × 3284% (chance 41%)5.1%
Latin49 × 3273% (chance 38%)5.7%

All three have permutation p below 0.01. It also holds outside Indo-European (the nearest neighbour is a family member for 25 to 53% of those languages, against 5 to 6% by chance), driven by Cebuano–Tagalog, Kannada–Telugu–Malayalam and Finnish–Hungarian, and inside Indo-European by branch (77 to 81% against 23%).

No language is a hub. The most central are analytic Indo-European languages with small vocabularies, and the anchor always moves up: English is first when it anchors, Hebrew 13th under the Hebrew anchor but 38th or 39th otherwise, Latin 18th to 41st depending on the anchor. Closeness to the centre tracks vocabulary size (rho 0.42 to 0.62). The Hebrew–Arabic pairing is not reliable (8th, 18th and 18th nearest to Hebrew under the three anchors).

Centrality, English anchor
2 · Ancient languages, 147 Indo-European

Distance is the share of 170 concepts where two languages have no common cognate. Each top-level clade counts once, so well-sampled clades do not decide the ranking. 40 of the languages are historical.

Historical, average distance0.787Modern, average distance0.818Older nearer the centre in7 of 7 cladesWithin-clade advantage+0.020 (p = 0.0005)

Ranks of 147, 1 is most central: Latin 1, Old French 4, Old Church Slavonic 11, Ancient Greek 20, Younger Avestan 28, Early Vedic 31, Classical Armenian 33, Tocharian B 41, Old Irish 91, Hittite 130. The most peripheral are modern, strongly diverged languages (Bengali, Marathi, Khowar, Bhojpuri, Urdu). Hittite, the earliest branch, is far out, as an early split predicts.

Is a known ancestor nearer to its descendants than they are to each other?
AncestorTo descendantsAmong them
Latin, 16 Romance0.3940.307
Early Vedic, 17 Indic0.6870.599
Ancient Greek, 5 Hellenic0.4560.235
Old Church Slavonic, 17 Slavic0.2000.245
Old Swedish, 7 North Germanic0.1820.200
Old Irish, 2 Goidelic0.2310.247

Latin and Vedic are farther from their descendants than those descendants are from each other, because the descendants share innovations the older language lacks (Romance comes from spoken Latin, not literary Latin). So even for a real ancestor, closeness to the centre would not identify it.

Clade-balanced distance, lower is nearer the centre
3 · Word lists, about 10,000 languages

ASJP has 40-word lists. 10,027 languages have at least 28 of the items, and 491 of them are extinct. In the 43 families with enough living and extinct members (350 extinct languages), extinct languages are nearer the centre of their family in only 17 of 43 families. The average advantage is negative (−0.018, or −0.004 weighted by number of extinct languages), and the permutation test gives p = 1.0. Large families are mixed: Pama-Nyungan +0.008, Afro-Asiatic +0.007, Indo-European +0.003, Austronesian −0.011.

So "older is nearer the centre" is supported where the old languages are genuinely ancient and carefully studied (Indo-European) and not detectable here. ASJP's extinct languages are mostly ones recorded in recent centuries, so the age gap is small, and 40 transcribed words is a crude measure.

What this adds up to

Languages share a structure that tracks ancestry, across 49 languages and nine families. Within Indo-European, older attested languages sit nearer the middle. No test finds a single root language, and the best-known ancestor, Latin, is not nearer to its descendants than they are to each other. Not covered: Sanskrit and Ancient Greek meaning shapes (no text corpus reachable), languages outside these datasets, and languages with no written records.

Not supported

Latin and Hebrew are not at the centre

With the same text for every language (340,000 words each), Latin ranks 20th of 28 for closeness to the others and Biblical Hebrew 27th. Neither is among the ten most central in more than 1% of resamples. After removing the effect of vocabulary size, Latin is mid-table (14th) and Hebrew stays near the edge (25th). So Latin is not a hub, but it is not an outlier either. Details are on the Root tab.

Hive Academy lab note · translation test

Can the shape translate words?

Source-language text was cut down and aligned to a full-size language by rotation. Share of held-out words whose translation comes first / in the top five, with 100 known word pairs as anchors (chance is 0.04%).

Source wordsHebrew → ArabicLatin → SpanishNo anchors (Heb→Ara)
20k0.9% / 4%0.0% / 1%0.2%
40k2.5% / 9%1.5% / 5%0.0%
80k8.4% / 20%5.8% / 17%0.1%
160k18.5% / 39%11.8% / 29%1.0%
320k24.2% / 49%14.7% / 40%1.4%

Below 40,000 words, first-choice accuracy stays under 3%: above chance but not useful. It becomes usable only from about 80,000 words. Without any anchors it fails. Still climbing at 320,000 words, so the ceiling is not found.

Control: no shared verses. Both languages cut to 150,000 words, first choice only. Disjoint halves of the Bible keep part of the signal. Old-half against new-half keeps little. Shuffled anchors give about 0.

PairSame versesRandom disjointFirst half vs secondShuffled anchors
Hebrew → Arabic21.5%11.2%3.9%0.2%
Latin → Spanish14.0%6.0%3.1%0.1%
Hebrew → English4.4%2.6%3.8%0.1%

So some of the signal is shared text, and some survives without it. Even the strictest split stays above chance, but the pairs are Bible-sized and the gold words are the easy, frequent ones.

What changed from the first version

  • The word list. Machine-made dictionaries that pivoted through English are gone. Words now come from NorthEuraLex, collected by linguists in each language's own spelling.
  • English. The first version said English led only because of the English pivot. With no pivot it is still at or near the top. Text volume is the likelier reason, and the concept list itself was drawn up from German glosses.
  • Basic vocabulary. The first version found no difference. That was wrong: its hand-made comparison list had kinship words on the wrong side.
  • Japanese. It was last because the dictionary gave it English loanwords. With proper words it is mid-table.
  • Coverage. NorthEuraLex covers northern Eurasia. Indonesian, Malay, Tagalog, Thai, Vietnamese and Afrikaans are no longer in the data; Latin, Basque, Georgian, Korean, Mongolian, Armenian and the Celtic and Turkic languages are.

What this cannot tell you

  • Latin here is not classical Latin. Its vectors come from Latin written recently, mostly Wikipedia and the web, and far less of it than the large languages have.
  • No Sumerian, Hittite, Sanskrit or Biblical Hebrew. No embeddings of this kind exist for them. Hebrew here is Modern Hebrew.
  • Text volume is measured coarsely. The word count is capped at 2.0M, and languages sit at the cap, so differences among the big languages are not controlled.
  • The concept list has a European starting point. It was compiled from German glosses, which may favour languages that divide the world the same way.
  • An Indo-European advantage is not robust. It shows in the -language run (p = ) and vanishes in the -language run (p = ).
  • Two runs, one trade-off. Keeping more languages leaves fewer shared concepts. The two rankings agree at for the languages in both.
  • Why Hebrew sits far out is not tested. Hebrew is written without vowels, so different words often share one spelling, which would blur its vectors. That is a guess.

How it was computed

  • Vectors: fastText cc.<lang>.300, trained separately for each language on Common Crawl and Wikipedia. Not pre-aligned.
  • Words: NorthEuraLex 0.9, 1,016 concepts. The first listed single word that appears among the language's 200,000 most frequent words.
  • Two complete blocks: . Every language has a word for every concept in its block.
  • Alignment: generalised Procrustes analysis with rotations and reflections. Each language is scored against the mean of the others.
  • Baseline: shuffles of each language's concept rows. Shared structure = 1 − distance ÷ shuffled distance.
  • Cross-check: a rotation-free score agrees with the Procrustes ranking at .
  • Shortcut: the leave-one-out mean reuses the full alignment. Checked against the exact version on four languages, it reads about 0.004 low for each.
